title: Overhaul of community centre operating model
subtitle: Fee assistance expansion, neighbourhood association rules, equity training, weekend hours study and reinvestment accountability for community centre programming.
overview: The Community and Infrastructure Services Committee recommended a broad update to how city-owned community centres are run. Staff said the current model, built on policies more than 20 years old, relies heavily on volunteers and leaves some centres under-programmed. The committee recommended the full package, as amended, on a recorded vote {{vote:m1}}. Council still has to adopt it.

For residents, the main changes are expanded help with costs. From fall 2023, the Leisure Access fee assistance program and the Inclusion Support Worker program would cover programs run by all Neighbourhood Associations at city-owned centres, with costs built into the 2024 operating budget. Staff would also review program registration, including ActiveNet, plan a city-wide promotional campaign, and prepare an issue paper on opening centres on weekends and earlier on weekday mornings.

Neighbourhood Associations would face new conditions of affiliation, including published equity, diversity and inclusion policies, periodic board training, and financial reporting and a published reinvestment policy for larger associations. City staff keep final say over space bookings. Staff are to report back before the end of the 2026 Council term. Staff said they would provide further information before Council's June 26 meeting.

decisions.item: Fee assistance and inclusion support expansion
decisions.detail: The committee recommended that from fall 2023 the Leisure Access program and the Inclusion Support Worker program cover all Neighbourhood Association programs at city-owned community centres, with costs built into the 2024 operating budget.

The committee recommended new affiliation conditions: published equity, diversity and inclusion policies, periodic city-funded board training, use of the Inclusion Support Worker program, and inviting the ward councillor and a staff member to board meetings and annual general meetings.

The committee recommended that associations with more than $20,000 in prior-year revenue report revenue, expenses and reserves annually and publish a policy on reinvesting net revenues, and that unspent funds go to the City if an association ceases operating.
The committee recommended updating the non-profit booking guidelines to recognize the variety of programs needed and to confirm that city staff have final authority over space allocation.
The committee recommended an issue paper for the 2024 budget process on the staffing and cost of opening centres on weekends and earlier on weekday mornings, possibly phased over several years.

The committee recommended a review of program registration processes including ActiveNet, a city-wide promotional campaign developed with associations, and a trial multi-year partnership agreement with one larger association.
The committee recommended reviewing the booking and affiliation policies every five years and a staff status update before the end of the 2026 Council term.

debate: Staff argued the current model puts a heavy burden on volunteers, leaves some centres under-used, and does not match resident priorities such as mental health and services for vulnerable people. They stressed the problem is the 20-year-old policies, not the volunteers.

A delegate who is a past association president raised concerns about the clause giving staff final say over space allocation, citing a long-standing understanding of guaranteed association hours, but supported the proposed partnership agreements. Staff replied that staff already hold final say and the change mainly clarifies wording.

Councillors disagreed on how far the City should oversee association reserves. Supporters wanted accountability for money generated at city assets. Others warned that requiring reinvestment plans to be satisfactory to the City could cause conflict with associations that were not consulted. The wording was withdrawn after staff agreed to address it in a fuller policy report later in the year.

Several councillors raised the burden on volunteers, so the fixed two-year equity training requirement was changed to training done periodically. One councillor also asked that fee assistance and inclusion support reach associations running programs outside city centres; staff said they would review this before the June 26 Council meeting.

Councillors asked for data on centre size, catchment areas and associations that have folded, to show inequities between neighbourhoods. Staff agreed to provide some of this information before Council's meeting.
